node.label: Ibn Khaldun
node.date_label: First Muqaddimah draft (1377) · Composition and revision of the larger Kitab al-Ibar in Tunis (1378–1382) · Final dated material in the surviving autobiography (1405)
node.description: A fourteenth-century historian formed within the intellectual and political worlds of the Islamic West. The Muqaddimah’s methodological introduction tests historical reports against social and political conditions. Its analysis of solidarity and authority offers a comparative question for historical sociology without making him a displaced modern European founder. Simon distinguishes the initial draft, later work on the larger history, and the surviving autobiography. Hannoum’s 2026 reading places colonial remakings alongside earlier Islamic receptions, keeping the transmission of his work a historical problem in its own right.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Muqaddimah (first draft November 1377); Kitab al-Ibar (larger-history composition/revision in Tunis 1378–1382); autobiography/at-Taʿrif (surviving continuation throughMay 1405). Modern reception is dated separately.
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: selected pages of Princeton’s translated author-text excerpt; Simon pp. 64–65 and 99–103; Stanford section 15; Hannoum’s selected sections. The Arabic originals and the larger history/autobiography themselves are unread; their writing chronology is mediated through Simon. Three separate writing milestones are shown, without turning modern translations into original contributions or assigning an invented single publication date. The 1405 point marks the final dated autobiographical material, not a confidently dated completion. Modern field comparisons do not establish direct intellectual descent, and this entry does not stand for all Islamic historiography.

This is an earlier contribution to problems of historical explanation, not membership in a modern analytic school.
